lead: A flat belt is a loop of flexible material that grips a pulley by friction over part of its rim. The driver pulls the tight side; the slack side returns. The two tensions are tied by T₁/T₂ = e<sup>μθ</sup>, so the belt can pull only as hard as friction allows. Design means choosing a width b so that the tight-side tension plus the centrifugal tension stays below the safe strength σbt. Flat belts drive line shafts, conveyors and small machines where the shafts are far apart and some slip is acceptable.
prereq: You need: belt materials, thickness and density from flexible drives and belt materials, and direct stress and the factor of safety from the design foundations.

sections.h3: Grip and the arc of contact

blocks.text: A flat belt transmits power only where it touches the pulley. The driver pulls the tight side and feeds the slack side. The arc of contact (also called the angle of lap) is the angle over which the belt touches a pulley. In an open drive the smaller pulley has the smaller arc, so with the same μ on both pulleys it slips first and sets the friction limit. In a crossed drive the two arcs are equal.

Use d and D for the small and large pulley diameters in metres, C for the centre distance in metres, and N₁, N₂ for speeds in rpm. Ignoring slip, N₁d = N₂D. With slip fraction s, N₂ = N₁(d/D)(1 − s); s is the fraction of belt speed lost.

blocks.where: θ is the arc of contact on the smaller pulley of an open belt, in degrees; d and D are the pulley diameters and C the centre distance, all in the same unit. The larger pulley gets 180° + 2 sin⁻¹((D − d)/(2C)).
θ is the arc of contact of a crossed belt, the same on both pulleys; the belt crosses between them and the pulleys turn in opposite directions.

blocks.text: Convert θ to radians before using e<sup>μθ</sup>. Belt length for an open drive is L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C). For a crossed drive, L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D + d)²/(4C).

Let T₁ and T₂ be the tight-side and slack-side tensions that produce friction, in N. The belt also carries the centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> = m v² on both sides, where m is the belt mass per metre in kg/m and v is belt speed in m/s; for width b and thickness t in metres and density ρ in kg/m³, m = ρbt. So the total pull in the tight side is T₁ + T<sub>c</sub>.

blocks.where: μ is the coefficient of friction; θ is the arc of contact on the smaller pulley in radians; e = 2.71828…, the base of natural logarithms.

blocks.text: The ratio comes from the balance of one small piece of belt on the rim:

Take a small piece of belt on the rim, subtending dθ.
Tensions: T on the slack end, T + dT on the tight end.
Radial balance: dN = T dθ   (the two pulls each lean in by dθ/2)
Limiting friction: dT = μ dN = μ T dθ
So dT/T = μ dθ. Integrate from T₂ to T₁ over 0 to θ:
ln(T₁/T₂) = μθ,  that is  T₁/T₂ = exp(μθ)
blocks.where: Assumptions: friction is at its limit over the whole arc, μ is constant, and the belt is thin and does not stretch. If T₁ and T₂ are total tensions that include T<sub>c</sub>, the result reads (T₁ − T<sub>c</sub>)/(T₂ − T<sub>c</sub>) = e<sup>μθ</sup>, because centrifugal force carries T<sub>c</sub> without pressing the belt on the rim.

blocks.text: The safe tension is T = σbt, where σ is the safe stress (already reduced for the joint). The tight side carries T₁ plus T<sub>c</sub>, so T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> ≤ T. Power is P = (T₁ − T₂)v. The initial tension set when the belt is fitted is T₀ = (T₁ + T₂)/2 + T<sub>c</sub>.

At fixed T and μθ, P = (1 − 1/e<sup>μθ</sup>)(T − m v²)v. Setting dP/dv = 0 gives T = 3m v²: maximum power comes when T<sub>c</sub> = T/3, at v = √(T/(3m)). For the 80 mm belt of the worked example, T = 2000 N and m = 0.8 kg/m, so v = 28.9 m/s and the peak is 22.6 kW.

items: v = πdN₁/60 from the smaller pulley.
θ of the smaller pulley, in radians.
T₁ − T₂ = P/v, then T₁ and T₂ from the ratio.
m = ρbt and T<sub>c</sub> = m v².
Solve T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> = σbt for b.
Round b up to a standard width; check the stress and T₀. Make the pulley face about a quarter wider than the belt.

blocks.text: Creep is the stretch on the tight side and contraction on the slack side. It makes the driven pulley lag slightly even with good friction. Slip is gross sliding when T₁/T₂ exceeds e<sup>μθ</sup>. Both reduce the velocity ratio. A flat belt is chosen when some slip is acceptable and the shafts are far apart.

figure.caption: Power the 80 mm belt of the worked example can carry at each belt speed. At 15.08 m/s it carries 16.07 kW, more than the 15 kW needed; its peak, 22.56 kW, comes at 28.87 m/s where centrifugal tension is a third of the safe tension.

examples.question: A 15 kW motor at 1440 rpm drives a line shaft at 480 rpm through an open flat belt. The pulley diameters are 200 mm and 600 mm, the centre distance is 2 m, μ = 0.3, belt thickness is 10 mm, density is 1000 kg/m³, and the safe stress is 2.5 N/mm². Find the belt width and the initial tension.
steps: Check the velocity ratio without slip: N₁d = 1440 × 0.200 = 288 and N₂D = 480 × 0.600 = 288. The speeds match the diameters.
Driving tension difference: T₁ − T₂ = P/v = 15 000/15.08 = 994.72 N.
Safe tension: T = σbt = 2.5 × b × 10 = 25b N (σ in N/mm², b and t in mm).
Strength condition: T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> = T, so 1696.9 + 2.274b = 25b, 22.726b = 1696.9 and b = 74.67 mm.
Take the standard width b = 80 mm. Check: m = 0.8 kg/m, T<sub>c</sub> = 181.9 N, pull = 1696.9 + 181.9 = 1878.8 N, stress = 1878.8/800 = 2.35 N/mm² < 2.5 N/mm².
examples.answer: The belt must be at least 74.67 mm wide; use a standard 80 mm belt, which runs at 2.35 N/mm². Fit it with an initial tension of about 1381 N.
examples.check:
import math
P, N1, d, D, C, mu, t, rho = 15000.0, 1440.0, 0.2, 0.6, 2.0, 0.3, 0.01, 1000.0
v = math.pi*d*N1/60
th = math.pi - 2*math.asin((D - d)/(2*C))
k = math.exp(mu*th)
T2 = (P/v)/(k - 1); T1 = T2 + P/v
b = T1/(25.0 - rho*t/1000*v**2)
Tc80 = rho*0.08*t*v**2
print(round(v, 2), round(math.degrees(th), 2), round(k, 4), round(T2, 1), round(T1, 1), round(b, 2))
print(round(Tc80, 1), round((T1 + Tc80)/800, 2), round((T1 + T2)/2 + Tc80, 1))

traps: Using 180° as the arc of contact. Use the smaller pulley’s arc: 168.52° in the worked example.
Feeding degrees into e<sup>μθ</sup>. Convert θ to radians first; 0.3 × 168.52 would give e<sup>50.6</sup>.
Forgetting T<sub>c</sub>. Without it the worked example gives b = 1696.9/25 = 67.9 mm, a belt that would really run at 2.73 N/mm², above the safe 2.5 N/mm².
Mixing millimetres and metres in m = ρbt. Use metres, or keep b in mm and write m = 0.010b as the worked example does.
Treating T₁ alone as the safe tension. The strength limit is T₁ + T<sub>c</sub> = σbt.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> and define each term.
quiz.a: T<sub>c</sub> = m v²; m is the belt mass per metre in kg/m and v is the belt speed in m/s.

quiz.q: Why does maximum power occur when T<sub>c</sub> = T/3?
quiz.a: For fixed T and μθ, P = (1 − 1/e<sup>μθ</sup>)(T − m v²)v. Setting dP/dv = 0 gives T − 3m v² = 0, so m v² = T/3. Below this speed the belt moves too slowly; above it, centrifugal tension uses too much of the safe strength.

quiz.q: An open belt has d = 150 mm, D = 450 mm and C = 1.5 m. Find the arc of contact on the small pulley in radians.
A flat belt drive transmits the same power at a very low speed and at a very high speed. Explain why both need a wider belt than the speed for maximum power.
quiz.a: At low speed, P = (T₁ − T₂)v needs a large tension difference, so T₁ is high. At high speed, T<sub>c</sub> = m v² is high, so less of the safe tension is left for T₁. In between, at v = √(T/(3m)), the belt width needed is the smallest.

quiz.q: Distinguish creep from slip in a belt drive.
quiz.a: Creep is elastic stretch and contraction of the belt as it moves from slack to tight side; it is always present. Slip is gross sliding when friction is insufficient; it is avoidable by design.

quiz.q: Why is the arc on the smaller pulley used in design, not the larger pulley's arc?
quiz.a: In an open drive the smaller pulley has the smaller arc, so with the same μ on both pulleys it has the smaller e<sup>μθ</sup> and slips first. If the belt does not slip there, it will not slip on the larger pulley. In a crossed drive both arcs are equal.

quiz.q: A belt transmits 10 kW at 12 m/s. e<sup>μθ</sup> = 2.0. Find T₁ and T₂.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern flat belts are often polyurethane or aramid-corded and run fast on small pulleys. Synchronous belts replace friction with teeth, so e<sup>μθ</sup> no longer limits them. Search "flat belt power rating" or "conveyor belt design" to go further.
